content_units: Hot-Water Pressure Likely Causes

Given your clues —   cold pressure is normal  ,   showers are worse than sinks  , and the   water heater is 11 years old   — the most plausible causes are the ones that restrict the   hot side specifically   and show up most at   higher-flow fixtures   like showers.
Most likely overall:   sediment-related restriction on the hot-water side   or   localized fixture restriction at shower heads/cartridges  .
Least likely overall:   main house pressure-reducing valve  , because that would usually affect   both hot and cold  .
Ranked Plausibility and What It Means
Rank   Cause   Why it fits your symptoms   What to inspect first   Replacement urgency

1     Sediment in water heater     An 11-year-old heater can accumulate mineral scale that reduces hot-water flow, especially noticeable at showers that demand more volume than sinks   Compare hot flow at tub spout, shower, bathroom sink, kitchen sink; drain a little from heater and look for sediment   Moderate; inspect before replacing

2     Clogged shower heads / hot-side shower cartridge restriction     Showers being worse than sinks strongly points to fixture-level restriction; mineral debris often collects in shower heads and balancing cartridges   Remove and inspect shower head screens; test flow with head removed; check shower cartridge if both showers are weak   Low; usually cheap fix

3     Partially closed hot-water shutoff valve     A half-closed valve on the heater outlet or nearby line can reduce only hot flow through the house   Verify heater inlet/outlet valves are fully open; check any utility-room isolation valves   Low; easy first check

4     Corroded galvanized section near utility room     If that galvanized segment is on the hot line, internal rust buildup could choke flow, especially at higher-demand fixtures   Identify whether that section is on hot, cold, or shared path; feel pipe routing and inspect unions/fittings for narrowing   Moderate to high if confirmed

5     Failing pressure-reducing valve     PRV problems usually affect whole-house pressure, not hot-only; normal cold pressure makes this a weak match   Only consider if pressure fluctuates house-wide or gauges show abnormal pressure swings   Low likelihood based on your description
First Checks Before Paying for Full Replacement
Start with the   lowest-cost, highest-signal checks   in this order:
1.   Test hot flow fixture by fixture
- Compare   hot-only   flow at:
- kitchen sink
- each bathroom sink
- each shower
- tub spout, if present
If   showers are much worse but sinks are acceptable  , the issue may be mostly   shower head/cartridge related  , not the whole system.
2.   Remove one shower head and retest
- If pressure improves a lot with the head removed, the problem is likely   clogging at the head  .
- If still weak, suspect   shower cartridge   or broader hot-side restriction.
3.   Check heater shutoff valves
- Confirm both the   cold inlet   and   hot outlet   valves at the water heater are fully open.
- Also check any valve near the utility room where prior work may have left one partially closed.
4.   Look for signs of heater sediment
- Briefly drain some water from the heater drain valve into a bucket.
- Heavy grit, rust flakes, or cloudy mineral debris supports the sediment theory.
- If hot flow improves after flushing, that is a strong clue.
5.   Identify that galvanized section
- If it is on the   hot outlet side  , it becomes much more suspicious.
- Galvanized pipe can corrode internally and create a severe bottleneck while looking fine outside.
Best Practical Interpretation
If I were ranking this for a 1998 two-bath house with your exact symptoms:
-   Most likely system cause:   sediment or debris affecting the   water heater/hot outlet path
-   Most likely cheapest fix:     shower head or cartridge cleaning/replacement
-   Most likely red herring:     pressure-reducing valve
A full water-heater replacement is   not the first move   unless you also have:
- poor hot flow at nearly   every   fixture,
- heater reliability problems,
- rusty/discolored hot water,
- rumbling/popping tank sounds,
- leaks or age pushing end-of-life.
Smart Next Steps
-   Inspect shower heads first   because showers are the worst-affected fixtures.
-   Confirm all hot-side valves are fully open  .
-   Flush/test the water heater for sediment   before approving replacement.
-   Have the plumber isolate the galvanized section   if the hot side remains weak after the easy checks.
- If hot flow is weak everywhere even after those checks, then   heater restriction or corroded hot piping   becomes the leading explanation.
